paras: The hanging-torture of Zachariah Johnson was an assault in May 1882 or shortly before, in which a mob in Union County, reported as in Indiana by most papers and in Arkansas by one, repeatedly hanged a Black man to force him to confess to a theft. Johnson survived, and the county sheriff and one or two deputies were reported arrested as participants. The story circulated as a short item in papers in North Carolina, Vermont and Pennsylvania.
Johnson, described as "colored," was suspected of having committed a theft, which he denied. The reports give no town, date, value or owner for the alleged theft.

According to the fullest account, printed by the Charlotte Home and Democrat, a mob "arrested him and took him into the woods" and demanded a confession; the Daily Republican says only that he "was caught in the woods." When Johnson said he was innocent, a rope was put around his neck and he was hanged from a tree limb until unconscious, then let down and revived. He was again ordered to confess "under penalty of death," and the hanging was repeated five times in all, the rope being released, in the Daily Republican's words, "when death was near."

After the fifth hanging, with Johnson still protesting his innocence, most of the mob, "disgusted with their work," refused to go on, and the group dispersed, leaving him to get away as best he could. The Middlebury Register said the mob left him "in a pitiable condition."

The sheriff and one of his deputies were reported arrested as participants, and the Daily Republican said it was Johnson who "had the sheriff and a deputy arrested as the perpetrators." The Juniata Sentinel and Republican instead counted the sheriff and two deputies under arrest. No report of a hearing, indictment or trial was found in the coverage, and none of the papers names the officers.

The coverage consisted of brief, undated items in papers far from Union County, the first in the Daily Republican on May 24 under the headline "Torturing a Negro." Two days later the Charlotte Home and Democrat ran the longest version, headed "A Negro Suspected of Theft Hanged Five Times," which spoke of "the most horrible suffering" of "the unfortunate negro" and called the affair "the outrage"; the Middlebury Register printed a condensed form of the same text the same day. On May 31 the Juniata Sentinel and Republican placed it among political paragraphs in its editorial column, describing officers who "took part in lynching a colored man."
No paper offered a defense of the mob, and the items reported the officers' arrest without comment on its result.

The papers disagree on the state: the Daily Republican placed the event in "Union county, Ark.," while the Charlotte, Middlebury and Juniata papers placed it in Indiana. Because all four items were distant reprints without a dateline, none is clearly better evidence on this point. They also differ on whether one deputy or two were arrested alongside the sheriff.

bases: A mob (with, per the reports, the sheriff and one or two deputies among it) repeatedly hanged a Black man to unconsciousness to extort a confession and then let him go alive (A2, A3, A4); A1 names only the sheriff and a deputy as perpetrators, which supports the record's police_violence reading, but the fuller accounts describe a mob.

Four brief out-of-state items (A1-A4) appear to derive from one undated dispatch, A2 and A3 nearly word for word; no local or follow-up report was found, and the items disagree on the state (Ark. in A1, Ind. in A2-A4).

framing.detail: The Charlotte Home and Democrat headlined 'A Negro Suspected of Theft Hanged Five Times' and wrote of 'the most horrible suffering' and 'the outrage'.
The Daily Republican ran it under 'Torturing a Negro'; the Middlebury Register ran a short unheaded version calling it 'the outrage'.
The Juniata Sentinel and Republican put it in an editorial column among political paragraphs, stating flatly that officers 'took part in lynching a colored man'.
